summary_html: Any person may submit a **third-party report** to child-protection authorities — and in New Mexico that report is not optional: every person who knows or reasonably suspects abuse or neglect must report it (NMSA 1978 § 32A-4-3(A)). CAPTA requires states to maintain mechanisms for intake, confidentiality, and immunity policies tied to federal funding.
authority_html: - **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — requires states to operate intake/report systems that accept voluntary reports and protect good-faith reporters

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Eckhardt v. Charter Hospital of Albuquerque, Inc.
key_cases.holding: The court held that a counseling center director owed the plaintiff a duty to maintain confidentiality and that good faith alone does not defeat a wrongful-disclosure claim, while identifying the child-abuse reporting statute and its immunity provision as a recognized exception to that duty.
key_cases.relevance: It identifies Section 32A-4-5(B) good-faith immunity as the affirmative defense that protects any person who reports suspected abuse.
key_cases.quote: Health-care providers must report actual or suspected cases of child neglect or abuse

key_cases.holding: The Court held that both privately and publicly employed licensed social workers are mandatory child-abuse reporters under NMSA 1978, Section 32A-4-3(A), so an alleged abuser's statements in private counseling sessions are not protected by the psychotherapist-patient privilege.
key_cases.relevance: It confirms that the reporting duty in Section 32A-4-3(A) runs to 'every person,' which is the statutory basis for third-party and voluntary reports in New Mexico.
key_cases.quote: both privately and publicly employed social workers are mandatory child abuse reporters, in light of the statutory history and the broadly inclusive terms of the Abuse and Neglect Act

mandatory_reporters: Licensed physicians, residents and interns examining, attending or treating a child (named in the statute as examples, not limits)
School employees (includes employees of a school district or a public school)
Social workers acting in an official capacity
Clergy, as to information that is not privileged as a matter of law
reporting_details: In New Mexico every person who knows or has a reasonable suspicion that a child is abused or neglected must report it immediately to a local law enforcement agency, to CYFD (Statewide Central Intake, 1-855-333-7233), or, for an Indian child residing in Indian country, to a tribal law enforcement or social services agency, and failing to report is a misdemeanor (NMSA 1978 § 32A-4-3(A), (F)). A finding that a pregnant woman is using or abusing drugs, made pursuant to an interview, self-report, clinical observation or routine toxicology screen, does not alone form a sufficient basis to report child abuse or neglect, and a volunteer, contractor or staff member of a hospital or freestanding birthing center shall not make a report based solely on that finding; notification of a plan of safe care goes to the health care authority and is not a report of abuse or neglect (NMSA 1978 § 32A-4-3(G)–(I), as amended by Laws 2025, ch. 156).
